Subject to any international management / trade controls

documentation.range: This species is found in southern Thailand, Malaysia (Malay Peninsula, Sabah, Sarawak, Labuan), Brunei, and Indonesia (Sumatra, Kalimantan, and Riau, Pini, Siberut, Lingga, Bangka, and Serasan Islands) (Helgen 2005). There are only a few records of this species from northern Sumatra. This is a lowland species occurring up to 1,200 m (Hawkins 2018).
documentation.population: The species is rare throughout most of its range, with the exception of Danum Valley, Sabah, Malaysia, where it is more common (Emmons 2000, Hawkins 2018).
documentation.habitats: The only nocturnal treeshrew, this arboreal species is found largely in primary forest (Hawkins 2018). However, on Borneo it has been observed in secondary forests and in gardens (Payne et al. 1998). Ptilocercus lowii forages on tree trunks for insects and fruit, and it consumes large amounts of fermented floral nectar (Wiens et al. 2008, Hawkins 2018). It nests communally with family groups in large dipterocarp trees (Hawkins 2018).
documentation.threats: The major threat to this arboreal species is loss of forest-canopy habitat due to agricultural expansion and conversion of land to non-tree crops. It survives in older (>5 years) mosaics of natural forest and tree plantations (Han et al. 2007, R. Stuebing pers. comm.). Borneo and Sumatra are both experiencing high rates of deforestation driven by the oil palm industry (Miettinen et al. 2016). The densely populated Malay Peninsula faces additional anthropogenic threats, including fragmentation due to large highways, human-wildlife conflict near urban centers, and pollution (Azlan 2006, Tee et al. 2018, Jambari et al. 2019).
documentation.measures:
It occurs in a few protected areas, including Danum Valley (Sabah, Malaysia), Bukit Lambir (Sarawak, Malaysia) and Pasoh Forest Reserve (Peninsular Malaysia), and some nearby offshore islands of Lumut-Sitiawan area, Perak (Peninsular Malaysia). A substantial colony has also been discovered (2006) in a forest remnant of an Acacia mangium plantation in the Bintulu Division, Sarawak (Han et al. 2007, R. Stuebing pers. comm.).
It is listed on CITES Appendix II. As the two subspecies (P. l. lowii and P. l. continentis) face different threats in different regions, they may require separate conservation interventions (Juman et al. 2021), especially as they are the only extant members of this distinctive family of treeshrews.
documentation.rationale: Although this species is rare and may be affected by severe deforestation throughout its lowland forest habitat, it shows some adaptability, for example, by occurring in plantations. It is unlikely that it has undergone declines sufficient to warrant listing in a threatened category, it has a wide distribution range and occurs in at least one protected area. It is therefore assessed as Least Concern.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: This species was assigned to the family Ptilocercidae by Shoshani and McKenna (1998), based on its possession of a number of unique external, craniodental and postcranial characters (Helgen 2005). This placement has recently been corroborated by molecular data (Janecka et al. 2007). Two subspecies are currently recognized: P. lowii lowii Gray, 1848 from Borneo and the offshore islands of Labuan and Serasan, and P. lowii continentis Thomas, 1910 from the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, and the offshore islands of Bangka, Lingga, Karimunbesar, Siberut, and Pini (Helgen 2005). These subspecies exhibit some morphological divergence, and individuals from the Mentawai islands (Siberut) are craniometrically distinct from the other populations (Juman et al. 2021). Future molecular and morphological research may support the recognition of two or more species.
